questions.explanation: « Bonjour » is the standard daytime greeting, literally 'good day'. In the evening it becomes « bonsoir ». Saying goodbye is « au revoir », which is the option most often confused with it.
« Merci » is thank you. The reply is « de rien » or « je vous en prie », which is the 'you're welcome' option here — a natural pairing to learn together rather than separately.
« Au revoir » literally means 'until the seeing again', which is why it works for any parting. « À demain » is specifically 'see you tomorrow', and that is the near-miss option here.

questions.stem: What does « s'il vous plaît » mean?
questions.explanation: « S'il vous plaît » is the polite 'please', literally 'if it pleases you'. With someone you address as « tu » it becomes « s'il te plaît » — the same phrase with the informal pronoun swapped in.
« Une école » is a school. Note the article: « école » begins with a vowel, so 'the school' is « l'école » rather than « la école » — French avoids two vowel sounds meeting.
« Un livre » is a book. A library is « une bibliothèque », which catches people out because English 'library' and French « librairie » look alike — but « librairie » is a bookshop.
« La famille » is the family. Individual members are worth learning as a set: « le père », « la mère », « le frère », « la sœur ».
« Le frère » is the brother; « la sœur » is the sister. « Le père » is the father, which is the option nearest in sound and the one most often picked by mistake.
« La sœur » is the sister. The œ is a single letter in French, called 'e dans l'o', and it also appears in « cœur » (heart) and « bœuf » (beef).
« Le pain » is bread. It looks exactly like the English word 'pain' and means nothing of the sort — one of the first false friends a French student meets.

« L'eau » is water, and it is feminine: « une eau minérale ». The spelling is worth noting because 'eau' is pronounced as a single 'o' sound, a pattern that repeats in « beau », « bateau » and « chapeau ».
« Le fromage » is cheese. Fruit is « le fruit », which is the closest option and an easy slip when reading quickly.
« Rouge » is red — the same root as English 'rouge' for red make-up, which makes it one of the easier colours to fix in memory.
« Vert » is green, and it shares a root with English 'verdant'. The feminine form adds an e: « verte », and the t is then pronounced.
« Noir » is black; « blanc » is white and « bleu » is blue. « Bleu » is the trap here, since it looks more like English 'blue' but is a different colour from the one being asked about.

questions.stem: How do you say 'three' in French?
questions.explanation: « Trois » is three. Two of the wrong options are built from the same root and are the standard confusion: « treize » is thirteen and « trente » is thirty.

questions.stem: How do you say 'ten' in French?
questions.explanation: « Dix » is ten. « Deux » (two) and « douze » (twelve) both begin with the same letter and are the usual mix-ups, so the numbers are worth drilling as a whole set rather than individually.
« Aujourd'hui » is today. « Hier » is yesterday and « demain » is tomorrow. The apostrophe is part of the spelling and is not optional.
« Demain » is tomorrow. Watch for « le matin », which means morning — the two are unrelated despite looking similar to an English eye.
« Une maison » is a house. « Une chambre » is a bedroom and « une pièce » is a room, so the English 'room' does not map onto one French word.

questions.stem: How do you say 'I am hungry' in French?
questions.explanation: French uses « avoir » (to have) for hunger, thirst, cold and age, where English uses 'to be'. So it is literally 'I have hunger'. Translating 'I am' directly gives « je suis faim », which no French speaker says.

questions.stem: How do you say 'my name is Alex' in French?
questions.explanation: « Je m'appelle » literally means 'I call myself' — a reflexive verb, where the action comes back to the speaker. English has no equivalent structure here, which is why a word-for-word translation fails.

questions.stem: How do you say 'thirteen' in French?
questions.explanation: « Treize » is thirteen. It sits between « douze » and « quatorze », and is easily confused with « trois » (three) and « trente » (thirty), which share its opening sound.

questions.stem: How do you say 'she is a teacher' in French?
questions.explanation: French drops the article before a profession after « être »: « elle est professeure », not 'a teacher'. Adding « une » is the most common error, because English requires it.

questions.stem: What does « J'ai quinze ans » mean?
options: I have been here fifteen years
questions.explanation: Age uses « avoir » in French: literally 'I have fifteen years'. Leaving off « ans » is a real error rather than a shortcut — « j'ai quinze » on its own means nothing.

questions.stem: How would you ask 'how are you?' politely?
questions.explanation: « Comment allez-vous ? » is the formal form, using « vous ». « Comment tu vas ? » and « ça va ? » are informal and belong with friends or family. Choosing between « tu » and « vous » is a social decision, not a grammatical one.

questions.stem: What does « Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît » mean?
options: I would like a coffee, please
questions.explanation: « Je voudrais » is 'I would like' — a conditional form, and far more polite than « je veux » ('I want'), which sounds blunt to a French ear. This is the phrase to use in any café.

questions.stem: What does « Où sont les toilettes ? » mean?
questions.explanation: « Où » means where, « sont » is 'are'. Note that « toilettes » is always plural in French. « Où » with an accent is 'where'; « ou » without one is 'or', and the accent is the only thing separating them.

questions.stem: What does « Je ne comprends pas » mean?
questions.explanation: This is the single most useful sentence for a learner. The negative wraps the verb in « ne … pas », which is the standard French pattern and takes two words where English uses one.

questions.stem: How do you say 'the red car' in French?
questions.explanation: Two things at once: most French adjectives follow the noun rather than coming before it, and « voiture » is feminine so it takes « la ». Putting the colour first is the instinct English gives you, and it is wrong.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I have two sisters and one brother'?
options: J'ai deux sœurs et une frère
J'ai deux sœurs et un frère
J'ai deux sœur et un frère
Je suis deux sœurs et un frère
questions.explanation: Three things have to be right together: « avoir » rather than « être » for possession, the plural s on « sœurs », and « un » for the masculine « frère ». Each wrong option breaks exactly one of those.

questions.stem: Which is the correct way to say 'it is half past three'?
options: Il est trois heures et demi
Il est trois heures et demie
questions.explanation: Time uses « il est », and « demie » agrees with the feminine « heures », so it takes an e. The last option translates the English word order directly, which French does not allow for time.

questions.stem: Which sentence means 'there is a book on the table'?
options: C'est un livre sur la table
Il y a un livre sous la table
Il y a un livre sur la table
Il est un livre sur la table
questions.explanation: « Il y a » is the fixed expression for 'there is' or 'there are' — it does not change for plural. The final option is grammatically fine but says 'under the table', so read the preposition carefully.
